extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and students of the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for producing and evaluating scientific observations, descriptions, concept-formation (abstraction), and the proper use of hypotheses and induction. Emphasizes discriminating raw sensations from inferences and forming clear, appropriate general conceptions by comparison and trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation from inference
rubrics_metrics.description: What is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; that it be an observation, not an inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly separate what you directly perceive (sensations) from the inferences you draw about causes or objects. Examples: hearing a sound (perception) vs identifying it as a man's voice (inference); seeing colored sensations vs asserting you saw a particular person. Habitual or rapid inferences can be confounded with direct perception and must be inspected by reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report raw sensations separately from attributed objects
rubrics_metrics.description: In every act of what is called observation, there is at least one inference—from the sensations to the presence of the object; observation extends only to the sensations by which we recognize objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing an observation, state the immediate sensations (e.g., 'I had a visual sensation of a colored surface', 'I heard a sound') before asserting identification or cause. This makes clear which parts of a report are empirical sensations and which are interpretive attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that most 'errors of sense' are erroneous inferences, not faulty sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are none of them properly errors of sense; they are erroneous inferences from sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing apparent perceptual errors (optical illusions, hallucinations), treat the raw sensory input as genuine and look to the judgment/inference that misattributes cause. Examples: kaleidoscope and cross-finger touch illusions—sensations genuine, deception arises in judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the logic of observation a discrimination task
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic of observation consists solely in a correct discrimination between that which has really been perceived, and that which is an inference from the perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For methodological clarity, identify and remove all inferential content from observational claims when preparing data for inductive reasoning. The remaining pure perceptions (sensations, feelings) are the empirical basis; inferences require separate treatment under induction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly acknowledge deductive steps within descriptions/measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many descriptive acts (e.g., asserting an animal measures ten feet from forehead to tail) are conclusions from reasoning, involving mathematical or deductive premises; the fact asserted is not an immediate perception but a conclusion from observed marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measurements or calculated quantities are reported, indicate the instruments, intermediate propositions (e.g., arithmetic), and the deductive steps used. Treat these as partly observational (minor premises) and partly inferential (deductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adequate repetition/number of instances to eliminate chance
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition collected from particulars may be more certainly true than any one of the particular propositions from which it was inferred, provided their number was sufficient to eliminate chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generalizing, ensure a sufficient number of independent instances so that it is unlikely all underlying inferences were simultaneously erroneous. More observations can reduce the chance that the common inference is due to coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat colligation/hypothesis as preparatory to induction, not identical with it
rubrics_metrics.description: The Colligation of Facts (by hypotheses/conceptions) is no other than the ordinary process of finding by a comparison of phenomena in what consists their agreement; it is subsidiary to Induction, not Induction itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses (guesses or conceptions) to organize observed facts and reveal common circumstances; but remember that asserting a hypothesis that fits observed points is a description until you inductively generalize to unobserved cases. Avoid equating successful fitting with proof of general law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly mark when a description becomes an induction/generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition (e.g., 'the earth moves in an ellipse') is a description when it merely connects observed points; it becomes Induction only when it affirms that unobserved intermediate positions would also correspond to the ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formulating laws, state whether the claim is limited to observed data (description) or intended as a general claim about unobserved cases (induction). This clarifies inferential reach and what needs further justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form general conceptions by comparison and abstraction, not by arbitrary imposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions are obtained by way of comparison and abstraction from particular phenomena; the conception which represents a class is either evolved from the facts or supplied by prior experience, but in all cases arises through comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate classifying concepts through systematic comparison of instances. Be wary of imposing preexisting conceptions that have not been justified by the phenomena under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must be clear and appropriate to the object of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions, to be subservient to Induction, must be 'clear' and 'appropriate'—that is, they should correspond to real agreements among the phenomena and be suited to the specific investigative aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose concepts that capture the real, relevant agreements among instances for the particular question. A conception appropriate for one inquiry (e.g., color) may be inappropriate for another (e.g., internal structure). Avoid vague or ill-fitting abstractions ('notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ').

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the standard (type) for comparison intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying many objects we fix upon one object as a standard and compare others to it; the standard becomes the type from which abstractions arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately choose your comparison standard based on what features you intend to study. If the chosen type yields few agreements, be prepared to abandon it and select a different starting point; the process is tentative and iterative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to iterate conceptions—try and revise until fittings are explanatory
rubrics_metrics.description: We find the right conception by a tentative process, trying first one and then another until we hit the mark; if not satisfied, we change our path and generate a different set of general conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat abstraction and type-selection as an experimental, iterative procedure. Evaluate whether a conception leads to meaningful, widespread agreements; if not, refine or replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of conception is relative to the question being asked
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of appropriateness is relative to the particular object we have in view—conceptions that are appropriate for studying one property may be irrelevant for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the investigative goal first, then form or select conceptions that are likely to reveal agreements pertinent to that goal. Example: color-based classification may serve studies of pigmentation causes but not anatomy-based functional laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing instinctive/habitual judgments with evidence of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of inferring from sensations can be so powerful that the inference, performed with the speed and certainty of an instinct, is confounded with intuitive perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to notice and suspend immediate judgments (e.g., as drawing students learn to 'see' raw shapes) so that inferences do not masquerade as direct observation. Reflective analysis is required to reveal which parts of a report are habitual inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that conception-formation may itself be difficult and crucial
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of an inductive operation often depends principally on the skill with which we perform abstraction; bad abstraction makes bad induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest effort into forming precise, well-founded conceptions; historical failures (e.g., lack of polarity concept) show that absent or poorly formed conceptions can delay scientific progress. Evaluate abstraction quality as part of methodological appraisal.
